title: Annual ROC Filing Deadlines: What Every Company Needs to Track
excerpt: A practical rundown of the recurring filings every Indian company should have on its compliance calendar.
content:
Every company incorporated in India, whether a small private limited company or a large multinational subsidiary, has a set of recurring filings due to the Registrar of Companies (ROC) each year. Missing these deadlines can mean late fees, additional government fees calculated per day of delay, and in repeated cases, disqualification of directors. This article walks through the filings that most private limited companies need to plan for.

1. Appointment of auditor – Form ADT-1

Once shareholders confirm the appointment or re-appointment of the statutory auditor at the AGM, the company must intimate the Registrar within 15 days using Form ADT-1. This is often missed because it sits outside the main "annual filing" bundle, but it carries its own late fee if delayed.

2. Financial statements – Form AOC-4

Within 30 days of the AGM, the company's financial statements, along with the Board's Report and auditor's report, must be filed in Form AOC-4 (or AOC-4 XBRL, where XBRL filing applies).

3. Annual return – Form MGT-7 / MGT-7A

Within 60 days of the AGM, companies must file their annual return, capturing shareholding pattern, director details and other statutory information as it stood on the last day of the financial year.

4. Director KYC – Form DIR-3 KYC

Every individual holding a Director Identification Number (DIN) must complete their annual KYC, generally by 30 September following the financial year.

Building a compliance calendar

Every filing above is triggered by the AGM date. A practical way to stay on top of this is to map every filing backward from your AGM date at the start of the financial year, rather than tracking each form in isolation.

  • Confirm your AGM date as early as possible in the financial year.
  • Calendar ADT-1, AOC-4 and MGT-7/7A relative to that date, not the financial year-end.
  • Track DIR-3 KYC separately, since it runs on a fixed annual date regardless of your AGM.
  • Keep minutes books and registers updated through the year, so year-end filings aren't a scramble.

This overview is general in nature. Exact requirements depend on your company's class, financial year, and events during the year.

title: LLP vs Private Limited: Choosing the Right Structure
excerpt: How founders should weigh liability, compliance load and fundraising plans before incorporating.
content:
One of the first decisions a founder makes is also one of the hardest to reverse cheaply: which legal structure to incorporate under. Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs) and Private Limited Companies are the two most common choices for new Indian businesses.

Liability protection

Both structures offer limited liability to their owners. This is the main reason both have replaced traditional partnerships and sole proprietorships for most serious businesses.

Compliance burden

A private limited company must hold a minimum number of board meetings, file annual returns and financial statements, maintain statutory registers, and follow rules on director appointments, share transfers and capital changes. An LLP's compliance load is lighter.

Fundraising

If you plan to raise equity funding, issue ESOPs, or eventually list, a private limited company is almost always the right choice.

Taxation

LLPs and private limited companies are taxed differently — a question best answered with your tax advisor based on your specific revenue model.

A simple way to think about it

  • Choose an LLP for a professional services business with no plans to raise external equity.
  • Choose a private limited company if you plan to raise venture or angel funding, issue ESOPs, or scale toward an exit or IPO.

title: FEMA Compliance Basics for Foreign Investment in India
excerpt: What founders and finance teams should know before receiving foreign investment.
content:
When an Indian company receives investment from a foreign shareholder, or an NRI, the transaction is governed by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) and RBI regulations. Getting this wrong can create compounding penalties and complications for future fundraising.

Reporting foreign investment: Form FC-GPR

When a company issues shares to a foreign investor, it must report the allotment to the RBI through Form FC-GPR, filed via the FIRMS portal, generally within 30 days of allotment.

Reporting share transfers: Form FC-TRS

When existing shares change hands between a resident and a non-resident, the transaction is reported through Form FC-TRS, with pricing guidelines applying in both directions.

Pricing guidelines

FEMA requires share issuances and transfers involving non-residents to happen at a price determined under an accepted pricing methodology, certified by a CA, Merchant Banker, or practising CS.

Sectoral caps and the automatic route

Most sectors allow 100% FDI under the automatic route, needing only post-facto RBI reporting. Certain sectors require government approval before investment.

The Annual FLA Return

Any Indian company with foreign investment on its books must file the annual FLA Return with the RBI, typically by 15 July each year.

Practical takeaways

  • Confirm your sector is open under the automatic route.
  • Get a compliant valuation certificate before pricing any transaction.
  • File FC-GPR or FC-TRS within prescribed timelines.
  • Don't forget the annual FLA return.
